claim: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies investigating the acquisition of sequential motor skills in humans have revealed learning-related functional reorganizations of the cortico-striatal and cortico-cerebellar motor systems accompanied with an initial hippocampal contribution.
source: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies investigating the acquisition of sequential motor skills in humans have revealed learning-related functional reorganizations of the cortico-striatal and cortico-cerebellar motor systems accompanied with an initial hippocampal contribution.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research in the field, as indicated by the context of the abstract summarizing existing literature.

claim: Representations in dorsolateral striatum, prefrontal and secondary motor cortices are greater when executing consolidated sequences than untrained ones.
source: The results reveal that representations in dorsolateral striatum, prefrontal and secondary motor cortices are greater when executing consolidated sequences than untrained ones.
evidence: This claim is directly stated as a result of the study and is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Sequence representations in the hippocampus and dorsomedial striatum become less engaged after consolidation.
source: By contrast, sequence representations in the hippocampus and dorsomedial striatum becomes less engaged.
evidence: This claim is directly stated as a result of the study and is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Complementary sequence-specific motor representations evolve distinctively during critical phases of skill acquisition and consolidation.
source: Our findings show, for the first time in humans, that complementary sequence-specific motor representations evolve distinctively during critical phases of skill acquisition and consolidation.
evidence: This claim is directly stated as a conclusion of the study and is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Practice of an explicit motor sequence learning task leads to substantial within-session execution improvements.
source: While practice of an explicit MSL task leads to substantial within-session execution improvements, there is now ample evidence indicating that between-session maintenance of, and even increases in, performance can be observed after a night of sleep (Landry et al., 2016; Nettersheim et al., 2015), while performance is unstable and tends to decay during an equal period of wakefulness (Doyon et al., 2009a; Brawn et al., 2010; Nettersheim et al., 2015; Landry et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: Between-session maintenance of, and even increases in, performance can be observed after a night of sleep.
source: While practice of an explicit MSL task leads to substantial within-session execution improvements, there is now ample evidence indicating that between-session maintenance of, and even increases in, performance can be observed after a night of sleep (Landry et al., 2016; Nettersheim et al., 2015), while performance is unstable and tends to decay during an equal period of wakefulness (Doyon et al., 2009a; Brawn et al., 2010; Nettersheim et al., 2015; Landry et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: Performance is unstable and tends to decay during an equal period of wakefulness.
source: While practice of an explicit MSL task leads to substantial within-session execution improvements, there is now ample evidence indicating that between-session maintenance of, and even increases in, performance can be observed after a night of sleep (Landry et al., 2016; Nettersheim et al., 2015), while performance is unstable and tends to decay during an equal period of wakefulness (Doyon et al., 2009a; Brawn et al., 2010; Nettersheim et al., 2015; Landry et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: Sleep favors reprocessing of the motor memory trace, thus promoting its consolidation for long-term skill proficiency.
source: Therefore, it is thought that sleep favors reprocessing of the motor memory trace, thus promoting its consolidation for long-term skill proficiency (Fischer et al., 2002, see King et al., 2017; Doyon et al., 2018 for recent in-depth reviews).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies and reviews.

claim: Motor sequence learning is associated with the recruitment of an extended network of cerebral, cerebellar and spinal regions.
source: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies using General-Linear-Model (GLM) contrasts of activation have also revealed that MSL is associated with the recruitment of an extended network of cerebral (Hardwick et al., 2013), cerebellar and spinal regions (Vahdat et al., 2015a), whose contributions differentiate as learning progresses (Karni et al., 1998; Dayan and Cohen, 2011; Doyon et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior fMRI research studies.

claim: The contributions of brain regions to motor sequence learning differentiate as learning progresses.
source: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies using General-Linear-Model (GLM) contrasts of activation have also revealed that MSL is associated with the recruitment of an extended network of cerebral (Hardwick et al., 2013), cerebellar and spinal regions (Vahdat et al., 2015a), whose contributions differentiate as learning progresses (Karni et al., 1998; Dayan and Cohen, 2011; Doyon et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: Plastic changes occur within the initial training session, as well as during the offline consolidation phase.
source: In fact, plastic changes (Ungerleider et al., 2002; Doyon and Benali, 2005) are known to occur within the initial training session, as well as during the offline consolidation phase, the latter being characterized by a functional 'reorganization' of the nervous system structures supporting this type of procedural memory function (Rasch and Born, 2008; Born and Wilhelm, 2012; Albouy et al., 2013b; Dudai et al., 2015; Bassett et al., 2015; Fogel et al., 2017; Vahdat et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: The offline consolidation phase is characterized by a functional 'reorganization' of the nervous system structures supporting procedural memory function.
source: In fact, plastic changes (Ungerleider et al., 2002; Doyon and Benali, 2005) are known to occur within the initial training session, as well as during the offline consolidation phase, the latter being characterized by a functional 'reorganization' of the nervous system structures supporting this type of procedural memory function (Rasch and Born, 2008; Born and Wilhelm, 2012; Albouy et al., 2013b; Dudai et al., 2015; Bassett et al., 2015; Fogel et al., 2017; Vahdat et al., 2017b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research studies.

claim: Motor sequence learning activates a cortical, associative striatal and cerebellar motor network, which is assisted by the hippocampus during the initial 'fast-learning' phase.
source: More specifically, MSL is known to activate a cortical, associative striatal and cerebellar motor network, which is assisted by the hippocampus during the initial 'fast-learning' phase (Albouy et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: When approaching asymptotic behavioral performance after longer periods of practice, activity within the hippocampus and cerebellum decreases while activity within the sensorimotor striatum increases.
source: Yet, when approaching asymptotic behavioral performance after longer periods of practice, activity within the hippocampus and cerebellum decreases while activity within the sensorimotor striatum increases (Doyon et al., 2002), both effects conveying the transition to the 'slow-learning' phase.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Striatal regions are reactivated during sleep spindles.
source: Other studies have then shown that the same striatal regions are reactivated during sleep spindles (Fogel et al., 2017), hence contributing to the progressive emergence of a reorganized network (Debas et al., 2010; Vahdat et al., 2017b) that is further stabilized when additional MSL practice is extended over multiple days and weeks (Lehéricy et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Increases in activity could signal a greater implication of the circuits specialized in movement sequential learning per se, or could result from the inherent faster execution of the motor task.
source: For instance, increases in activity could not only signal a greater implication of the circuits specialized in movement sequential learning per se, but could also result from the inherent faster execution of the motor task.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference about the interpretation of activity changes.

claim: A decrease in activity could either indicate some form of optimization and greater efficiency of the circuits involved in executing the task, or could show the reduced recruitment of non-specific networks supporting the acquisition process.
source: Likewise, a decrease in activity could either indicate some form of optimization and greater efficiency of the circuits involved in executing the task (Wu et al., 2004), or could show the reduced recruitment of non-specific networks supporting the acquisition process.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference about the interpretation of activity changes, with one possibility supported by a citation.

claim: Large-scale activation differences associated with different learning phases do not necessarily provide direct evidence of plasticity related to the processing of a motor sequence-specific representation.
source: Therefore, even with the use of control conditions to dissociate sequence-specific from non-specific processes (Orban et al., 2010), the observed large-scale activation differences associated with different learning phases do not necessarily provide direct evidence of plasticity related to the processing of a motor sequence-specific representation (Berlot et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference about the limitations of GLM-based approaches, supported by citations.

claim: Plastic changes could occur locally without significant changes in the GLM-based regional activity level.
source: Furthermore, it is also conceivable that these plastic changes could even occur locally without significant changes in the GLM-based regional activity level.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference about the limitations of GLM-based approaches.

claim: Multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) has been proposed to evaluate how local patterns of activity are able to reliably discriminate between stimuli or evoked memories of the same type over repeated occurrences.
source: To address these specificity limitations, multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) has been proposed to evaluate how local patterns of activity are able to reliably discriminate between stimuli or evoked memories of the same type over repeated occurrences, hence allowing to test information-based hypotheses that GLM contrasts cannot inquire (Hebart and Baker, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research on MVPA methods.

claim: Extended training increased sequence discriminability in a network spanning bilaterally the primary and secondary motor as well as parietal cortices.
source: The authors showed that the extended training increased sequence discriminability in a network spanning bilaterally the primary and secondary motor as well as parietal cortices.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Wiestler and Diedrichsen, 2013).

claim: Representations of extensively trained sequences were identified in the contralateral dorsal premotor and supplementary motor cortices during preparation.
source: In another study (Nambu et al., 2015) that aimed to analyze separately the preparation and execution of sequential movements, representations of extensively trained sequences were identified in the contralateral dorsal premotor and supplementary motor cortices during preparation, while representations related to the execution were found in the parietal cortex ipsilaterally, the premotor and motor cortices bilaterally as well as the cerebellum.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Nambu et al., 2015).

claim: Representations related to the execution were found in the parietal cortex ipsilaterally, the premotor and motor cortices bilaterally as well as the cerebellum.
source: In another study (Nambu et al., 2015) that aimed to analyze separately the preparation and execution of sequential movements, representations of extensively trained sequences were identified in the contralateral dorsal premotor and supplementary motor cortices during preparation, while representations related to the execution were found in the parietal cortex ipsilaterally, the premotor and motor cortices bilaterally as well as the cerebellum.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research (Nambu et al., 2015).

claim: The regions carrying sequence-specific representations overlapped only partly with those identified using GLM-based measures.
source: In both studies, the regions carrying sequence-specific representations overlapped only partly with those identified using GLM-based measures, hence illustrating the fact that coarser differences in activation between novel and trained sequences does not necessarily provide evidence of plasticity for sequential information.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from prior research findings.

claim: Classification-based measures may have biased parametric statistical results by violating both the normality assumption and theoretical null-distribution.
source: However, the classification-based measures they used may have biased their parametric statistical results by violating both the normality assumption and theoretical null-distribution (Jamalabadi et al., 2016; Allefeld et al., 2016; Combrisson and Jerbi, 2015; Varoquaux, 2018) and may have thus been suboptimal in detecting representational changes (Walther et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on statistical methods.

claim: A large distributed set of regions displayed significant discriminability for both consolidated and new sequences, including the primary visual, as well as the posterior parietal, primary and supplementary motor, premotor and dorsolateral prefrontal cortices.
source: A large distributed set of regions (Figure 2) displayed significant discriminability, including the primary visual, as well as the posterior parietal, primary and supplementary motor, premotor and dorsolateral prefrontal cortices.
evidence: This claim is supported by the MVPA analysis results and reference to Figure 2.

claim: Discriminability between the consolidated sequences was significantly higher than that between the new sequences in bilateral sensorimotor putamen, thalamus and anterior insula.
source: Discriminability between the consolidated sequences was significantly higher than that between the new sequences in bilateral sensorimotor putamen, thalamus and anterior insula, as well as in the ipsilateral cerebellar lobule IX, posterior cingulate and parietal cortices, and contralaterally in the lateral and dorsal premotor, supplementary motor, frontopolar and dorsolateral prefrontal cortices in addition to cerebellar Crus I.
evidence: This claim is supported by the MVPA analysis results from the study.

claim: Discriminability between the consolidated sequences was significantly higher than that between the new sequences in the ipsilateral cerebellar lobule IX, posterior cingulate and parietal cortices.
source: Discriminability between the consolidated sequences was significantly higher than that between the new sequences in bilateral sensorimotor putamen, thalamus and anterior insula, as well as in the ipsilateral cerebellar lobule IX, posterior cingulate and parietal cortices, and contralaterally in the lateral and dorsal premotor, supplementary motor, frontopolar and dorsolateral prefrontal cortices in addition to cerebellar Crus I.
evidence: This claim is supported by the MVPA analysis results from the study.

claim: Discriminability between the consolidated sequences was significantly higher than that between the new sequences contralaterally in the lateral and dorsal premotor, supplementary motor, frontopolar and dorsolateral prefrontal cortices in addition to cerebellar Crus I.
source: Discriminability between the consolidated sequences was significantly higher than that between the new sequences in bilateral sensorimotor putamen, thalamus and anterior insula, as well as in the ipsilateral cerebellar lobule IX, posterior cingulate and parietal cortices, and contralaterally in the lateral and dorsal premotor, supplementary motor, frontopolar and dorsolateral prefrontal cortices in addition to cerebellar Crus I.
evidence: This claim is supported by the MVPA analysis results from the study.

claim: The pattern dissimilarity was higher for the new sequences in bilateral hippocampi as well as the body of the caudate nuclei, subthalamic nuclei, and cerebellar Crus II ipsilaterally.
source: By contrast, the pattern dissimilarity was higher for the new sequences in bilateral hippocampi as well as the body of the caudate nuclei, subthalamic nuclei, and cerebellar Crus II ipsilaterally.
evidence: This claim is supported by the MVPA analysis results from the study.

claim: Although striatal activity patterns differentiating newly acquired sequences were found in contralateral putamen, this discriminability was significantly larger for consolidated sequences in sensorimotor regions of the putamen bilaterally.
source: Although striatal activity patterns differentiating newly acquired sequences were found in contralateral putamen (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), this discriminability was significantly larger for consolidated sequences in sensorimotor regions of the putamen bilaterally.
evidence: This claim is supported by the MVPA analysis results and reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: No results survived multiple comparison correction in the univariate GLM analysis contrasting consolidated and new sequences.
source: We also conducted a univariate GLM analysis to contrast the consolidated and new sequences, but no results survived multiple comparison correction.
evidence: This claim is supported by the GLM analysis results from the study.

claim: The negative result in the univariate GLM analysis could be accounted for by the absence of smoothing of signals during preprocessing.
source: This negative result could be accounted for by the absence of smoothing of signals during preprocessing.
evidence: This claim is based on inference about methodological factors affecting the GLM analysis.

claim: The medial and lateral premotor areas as well as posterior parietal cortices bilaterally and contralateral somatosensory motor cortex show reliable discrimination of sequence-specific activity patterns for both the consolidated and novel sequences.
source: At the cortical level, it encompasses the medial and lateral premotor areas as well as posterior parietal cortices bilaterally and contralateral somatosensory motor cortex. These findings are consistent with earlier MVPA investigations (Wiestler and Diedrichsen, 2013; Nambu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by the MVPA analysis results from the study and is consistent with prior research.

claim: Similar discriminative power of motor sequence representations within the ipsilateral premotor and parietal cortices has previously been described.
source: Indeed, similar discriminative power of motor sequence representations within the ipsilateral premotor and parietal cortices has previously been described (Wiestler and Diedrichsen, 2013; Waters-Metenier et al., 2014; Waters et al., 2017), notably when the non-dominant hand is used for fine dexterous manual skills.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Significant neural representations for both learning stages were found in the contralateral primary motor and somatosensory (M1/S1) cortices, more specifically around the hand knob area.
source: Interestingly, we also found significant neural representations for both learning stages in the contralateral primary motor and somatosensory (M1/S1) cortices, more specifically around the hand knob area (Yousry et al., 1997) for which finger somatotopy is measurable using fMRI (Ejaz et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by the MVPA analysis results from the study and citations to prior research on anatomy and methods.

claim: The capacity to discriminate between sequences based upon signals from M1/S1 regions could simply be due to the stronger activity evoked by the first finger press in the sequence, and not to activity from the whole finger sequence.
source: Yet such an interpretation must be taken with caution, as it has recently been reported that the capacity to discriminate between sequences based upon signals from these regions could simply be due to the stronger activity evoked by the first finger press in the sequence, and not to activity from the whole finger sequence (Yokoi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The first finger effect cannot explain the pattern of results because, while the newly learned sequences began with different fingers, both consolidated sequences were discriminated despite the fact that the first finger presses were the same.
source: Yet although conjectural, we do not believe that such an effect can explain our pattern of results because, while the newly learned sequences began with different fingers, both consolidated sequences were discriminated despite the fact that the first finger presses were the same.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference from the experimental design and results.

claim: The spatial extent of the M1/S1 representation in this study was smaller compared with that found by Wiestler and Diedrichsen (2013).
source: Finally, while being located around the hand knob, the spatial extent of the M1/S1 representation in our study was smaller compared with that found by Wiestler and Diedrichsen (2013).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of the current study's results with prior research.

claim: Differences in the spatial extent of M1/S1 representation may be due to differences in design, notably in the uninterrupted repetition of the motor sequence during practice, and in the fact that none of the sequences engaged the thumb.
source: This may be due, however, to differences in our design, notably in the uninterrupted repetition of the motor sequence during practice, and in the fact that none of our sequences engaged the thumb, which has a more distinctive M1/S1 cortical representation than the individual fingers (Ejaz et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on inference about methodological factors and is supported by a citation to prior research on somatotopy.

claim: The first finger effect could explain the significant results observed in the map of new sequence discrimination, such as in a large extent of the dorsal ipsilateral cerebellum.
source: As other regions are expected to show finger somatotopic organization (Wiestler et al., 2011), this first finger effect could explain the significant results observed in the map of new sequence discrimination (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), such as in a large extent of the dorsal ipsilateral cerebellum.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from prior research on somatotopy and reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: A common cortical processing network, including non-motor primary and associative regions, carries sequential information across learning stages.
source: The conjunction of new and consolidated sequences discriminability maps further revealed that a common cortical processing network, including non-motor primary and associative regions, carries sequential information across learning stages, which can originate from visually presented instruction and short-term memory to motor sequence production.
evidence: This claim is supported by the MVPA analysis results from the study.

claim: The visual occipital cortices discriminate between sequences in both stages of learning, which could reflect the processing of the visual stimuli as low-level visual mapping of shapes.
source: Herein, the visual occipital cortices, which could reflect the processing of the visual stimuli as low-level visual mapping of shapes (Pilgramm et al., 2016; Miyawaki et al., 2008), as well as the ventro-temporal regions, known to support higher level Arabic number representation (Shum et al., 2013; Peters et al., 2015), were found to discriminate between sequences in both stages of learning (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the MVPA analysis results and citations to prior research.

claim: The ventro-temporal regions, known to support higher level Arabic number representation, were found to discriminate between sequences in both stages of learning.
source: Herein, the visual occipital cortices, which could reflect the processing of the visual stimuli as low-level visual mapping of shapes (Pilgramm et al., 2016; Miyawaki et al., 2008), as well as the ventro-temporal regions, known to support higher level Arabic number representation (Shum et al., 2013; Peters et al., 2015), were found to discriminate between sequences in both stages of learning (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by the MVPA analysis results and citations to prior research.

claim: The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex was suggested previously to process the sequence spatial information in working memory, preceding motor command.
source: The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, which also exhibited pattern discriminability, was suggested previously to process the sequence spatial information in working memory, preceding motor command (Robertson et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The cognitive processing required in the task, implying notably to switch between sequences, to maintain them in working memory and to inhibit competing ones, could have magnified the frontal associative representation.
source: In fact, we believe that the cognitive processing required in our task, implying notably to switch between sequences, to maintain them in working memory and to inhibit competing ones, could have magnified this frontal associative representation in our study.
evidence: This claim is based on inference about the cognitive demands of the task.

claim: The regions found to carry sequence information regardless of the learning phase show some overlap with the network known to be implicated in motor sequence learning, such as primary and secondary motor cortices.
source: In sum, the regions found to carry sequence information regardless of the learning phase in the present study show some overlap with the network known to be implicated in MSL, such as primary and secondary motor cortices, as typically revealed in activation-based studies (Doyon et al., 2009b; Hardwick et al., 2013; Dayan and Cohen, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the current study's results with prior research.

claim: Significant representations were also found in the occipital, temporal and insular cortices.
source: However, we also found significant representations in the occipital, temporal and insular cortices.
evidence: This claim is supported by the MVPA analysis results from the study.

claim: The discrepancy between MVPA and activation-based studies can be attributable to the shift from an activation-based inference to one based on the presence of sequential information in activity patterns, but also by the recruitment of additional regions for the processing of this information in stimuli and its maintenance in working memory required by the task.
source: This discrepancy can be attributable to the shift from an activation-based inference to one based on the presence of sequential information in activity patterns, but also by the recruitment of additional regions for the processing of this information in stimuli and its maintenance in working memory required by the task.
evidence: This claim is based on inference about the differences between methodological approaches.

claim: The contralateral premotor and bilateral parietal regions showed a stronger representation for consolidated sequences.
source: At the cortical level, we found that the contralateral premotor and bilateral parietal regions showed a stronger representation for consolidated sequences.
evidence: This claim is supported by the MVPA analysis results from the study.

claim: The tuning of neural populations in premotor and parietal regions to coordinated movements is consolidated early after learning.
source: This pattern suggests that the tuning of these neural populations to coordinated movements is consolidated early after learning (Makino et al., 2017; Yokoi et al., 2018; Pilgramm et al., 2016), as was previously observed when contrasting a sequence that underwent a longer training with new ones (Wiestler and Diedrichsen, 2013).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the current study's results and is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: No significant changes in representational magnitude were found in the contralateral primary somatosensory cortex after consolidation.
source: Importantly, no significant changes in representational magnitude were found in the contralateral primary somatosensory cortex after consolidation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the MVPA analysis results from the study.

claim: M1 representational geometry has been shown to be strongly shaped by ecological finger co-activations.
source: This is in line with the fact that M1 representational geometry has been shown to be strongly shaped by ecological finger co-activations (Ejaz et al., 2015), and to be resistant to extensive training of a sequence built on a new co-activation structure (Beukema et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: M1 representational geometry is resistant to extensive training of a sequence built on a new co-activation structure.
source: This is in line with the fact that M1 representational geometry has been shown to be strongly shaped by ecological finger co-activations (Ejaz et al., 2015), and to be resistant to extensive training of a sequence built on a new co-activation structure (Beukema et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The negative result in M1 complements the results of Figure 2, supporting that primary representation uncovered there might not reflect sequential features but the interaction of pre-existing somatotopic organization and single finger position in each sequences.
source: This negative result complements that of Figure 2, supporting that primary representation uncovered there might not reflect sequential features but the interaction of pre-existing somatotopic organization and single finger position in each sequences.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the current study's results and reference to Figure 2.

claim: The role of the motor cortex in motor sequence learning is undeniable, but its plasticity in consolidation is still debated.
source: While the role of the motor cortex in MSL is undeniable, its plasticity in consolidation is still debated (Omrani et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: After a M1 insult or even rapidly after M1 inactivation, a trained motor skill can still be expressed.
source: In fact, recent results revealed that after a M1 insult or even rapidly after M1 inactivation, a trained motor skill can still be expressed (Kawai et al., 2015; Bollu et al., 2018) arguing for its complementary, redundant and partially independent representation in subcortical regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Trained motor skills have complementary, redundant and partially independent representation in subcortical regions.
source: In fact, recent results revealed that after a M1 insult or even rapidly after M1 inactivation, a trained motor skill can still be expressed (Kawai et al., 2015; Bollu et al., 2018) arguing for its complementary, redundant and partially independent representation in subcortical regions.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from prior research findings.

claim: Significant differences at the subcortical level were found in bilateral putamen and more specifically in their sensorimotor regions.
source: Interestingly, significant differences at the subcortical level were found in bilateral putamen and more specifically in their sensorimotor regions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the MVPA analysis results from the study.

claim: The finding of increased representation in bilateral putamen after consolidation is consistent with findings from activation studies that reported increased functional activity after consolidation in this structure.
source: This is consistent with findings from activation studies that reported increased functional activity after consolidation in this structure (Debas et al., 2010; Albouy et al., 2013b; Debas et al., 2014; Fogel et al., 2017; Vahdat et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the current study's results with prior research.

claim: Regions of the basal ganglia are part of anatomical loops with afferents in primary and secondary motor cortices as well as efferents to the cortex via thalamic relays, and can show some degree of somatotopic organization.
source: As these regions of the basal ganglia are part of anatomical loops with afferents in primary and secondary motor cortices as well as efferents to the cortex via thalamic relays, these can show some degree of somatotopic organization (Nambu, 2011) that could contribute to the sequence discriminability, similarly to what is observed in the cortex (Yokoi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on anatomy and function.

claim: Significant representational differences were found in the bilateral thalami, which could reflect the relay of information between the cortex and cerebellum, striatum or spinal regions.
source: Significant representational differences were also found in the bilateral thalami, and could reflect the relay of information between the cortex and cerebellum, striatum or spinal regions (Haber and Calzavara, 2009; Doyon et al., 2009a).
evidence: This claim is supported by the MVPA analysis results and citations to prior research.

claim: Distinct representation levels were detected in the cerebellum, including ipsilateral Lobule IX, shown to correlate with sequential skill performance.
source: Finally, distinct representation levels were detected in the cerebellum, including ipsilateral Lobule IX, shown to correlate with sequential skill performance (Orban et al., 2010; Tomassini et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by the MVPA analysis results and citations to prior research.

claim: No significant difference was observed in Lobule V of the cerebellum that is known to carry finger somatotopic representations and to show global activation during practice.
source: However, no significant difference was observed in Lobule V of the cerebellum that is known to carry finger somatotopic representations (Wiestler et al., 2011) and to show global activation during practice (Doyon et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by the MVPA analysis results and citations to prior research.

claim: Only a few disparate regions showed lower sequence discrimination, namely the caudate nuclei, subthalamic nuclei and cerebellar Crus II ipsilaterally as well as bilateral hippocampi.
source: Concurrently with the positive representational differences in the above-mentioned areas, we found only a few disparate regions that showed lower sequence discrimination, namely the caudate nuclei, subthalamic nuclei and cerebellar Crus II ipsilaterally as well as bilateral hippocampi.
evidence: This claim is supported by the MVPA analysis results from the study.

claim: Hippocampal activation in early learning has formerly been hypothesized to support the temporary storage of new explicitly acquired motor sequence knowledge and to contribute to the reactivations of the distributed network during offline periods and sleep in particular.
source: Hippocampal activation in early learning has formerly been hypothesized to support the temporary storage of new explicitly acquired motor sequence knowledge and to contribute to the reactivations of the distributed network during offline periods and sleep in particular.
evidence: This claim is based on prior hypotheses in the field.

claim: The contribution of the hippocampus has been shown to be progressively disengaging after early learning.
source: Yet such contribution of the hippocampus has been shown to be progressively disengaging afterward (Albouy et al., 2013b), and thus our results are consistent with the idea of the hippocampus playing a transient supportive role in early MSL, notably in encoding sequential information (Davachi and DuBrow, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The results are consistent with the idea of the hippocampus playing a transient supportive role in early motor sequence learning, notably in encoding sequential information.
source: Yet such contribution of the hippocampus has been shown to be progressively disengaging afterward (Albouy et al., 2013b), and thus our results are consistent with the idea of the hippocampus playing a transient supportive role in early MSL, notably in encoding sequential information (Davachi and DuBrow, 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the current study's results and is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The findings of a differential implication of dorsomedial and dorsolateral striatum in sequence representation during learning and expression of a consolidated skill bring specificity to the changes in activity in these regions in the course of motor sequence learning described by earlier studies.
source: Our findings of a differential implication of dorsomedial and dorsolateral striatum in sequence representation during learning and expression of a consolidated skill bring specificity to the changes in activity in these regions in the course of MSL described by earlier studies (Lehéricy et al., 2005; Jankowski et al., 2009; François-Brosseau et al., 2009; Kupferschmidt et al., 2017; Corbit et al., 2017; Fogel et al., 2017; Reithler et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of the current study's results with prior research.

claim: The results uncover that the shift in activity in dorsomedial and dorsolateral striatum is consistent with animal studies showing a reorganization at the neuronal level in these regions.
source: Indeed, our results uncover that this shift in activity is consistent with animal studies showing a reorganization at the neuronal level in these regions (Costa et al., 2004; Yin et al., 2009; Miyachi et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of the current study's results with prior animal research.

claim: The present study was not designed to investigate the information content of hippocampal, striatal or cerebellar sequence representations.
source: While our results show regional magnitude of motor sequential information differs between consolidated and newly acquired memory traces, the present study was not designed to investigate the information content of hippocampal, striatal or cerebellar sequence representations.
evidence: This claim is an explicit statement about the study's design limitations.

claim: Information content of sequence representations was previously assessed at the cortical level for finger sequences.
